card werk-wording  [decided]
A card's words describe its own subject, not the session that wrote it
why: A card is read later, cold, by someone who needs to act on its subject. Session facts (who said what, what came before, what stage the conversation was at) are stale on arrival and carry no decision weight.

No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour and concepts. It does not name a command or a flag: the command form of an operation lives on one card under #werk-cli, and every other card names the operation instead. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.

The agent prompt states the card wording rules
why: Card text drifts back to session narration and code names when the agent that writes it does not see the rules. Putting the rules in the prompt every session loads costs nothing per card.

The prompt that every werk session and subagent loads states the wording rules of #werk-wording: a card describes its own subject, not the session that wrote it, and it stays at the level of the decision.

No program checks the text. The human read before accept stays the last gate.

This is not a state-transition rule. Wording applies to every add, edit, and retitle, not to one move between states.

=== werk-cli [decided] The CLI is the agent's interface to the map. Each command's form lives on one card under it
why: The agent has a shell and no other way to touch the map. One list of verbs, with each verb pointing at the card that defines it, lets a card describe an operation without naming a command.
pending: null
--- body
The CLI is the interface the agent uses to read and write the map. `werk help` prints every verb with its flags. A verb is a name for an operation. The rules of the operation live on one card. The form of the command — the verb, its flags and its output — lives on one card under this one. This card lists where each verb is.

Map content:
- add a card: #werk-cli-add
- change a decided card: #map-frozen
- place a card in the tree: #vi-levels
- link two cards, remove a link: #werk-cli-link
- set a status: #werk-cli-decide
- record when to revisit: #kill
- reopen, and what goes stale: #werk-cli-reopen
- clear a stale mark: #werk-cli-reopen
- dispute a source, clear the dispute: #vi-srcnode

Staged change:
- propose, accept, discard: #werk-cli-propose
- remove, restore: #werk-remove

Reading:
- list marked cards: #werk-cli-stale
- find open cards: #werk-find
- print one card, its neighbours and its stale trace: #werk-cli-show
- read another conversation, quote it: #werk-cli-recall
- read and write a card's notes: #werk-cli-notes

Sampling and prototypes:
- sample, sample-options, prototype: #werk-cli-sample

Build:
- plan, loop, build, run, gate, ticket: #werk-cli-build

Server:

A card that needs an operation names the operation and points at the card that defines it. It does not copy the verb name or its flags. A new operation gets a card first, then a line here.

A card under this one depends on the cards that define its operations. No card outside this subtree depends on a card inside it. So a change to a command or a flag never marks a design card stale.

=== vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape [decided] A separate shape grid defines each group's shape, and the diagram's cards must fit inside it
why: A group frame drawn as the bounding box of its cards has two defects. It reserves no cells for its own header strip, and its rectangle can cover a card that is not a member of the group. A shape grid uses the card-grid syntax at a coarser resolution, so the author declares each group's shape as its own checked artifact. Each card must then fit inside its group's declared cells. The checker enforces that rule, so layout does not decide it by chance. One group nests in another when its cells sit inside the other group's cells.
pending: null
--- body
The diagram gets a shape grid. A declared row or group type that reserves header-strip cells would fix only the header-space defect, not the containment defect, where a frame's rectangle swallows a card that is not its member. The containment defect is the real bug. See gap 2 on #vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps.

Seven parts define the shape grid:
- file location: a section in the same file as the diagram (#vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape-shape-grid-file-location)

- nesting: derived from shape-grid rectangle containment, never declared in text (#vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape-nesting-declaration-source)
- rectangle check scope: a parent's checked region is the union of its own cells plus descendants' (#vi-sysdiag-grid-groupshape-shape-rectangle-check-scope)

=== kill [decided] Every decision carries kill criteria: what must become true to revisit it
why: The author sets the revisit trigger when the decision is made. A later challenge only checks that trigger, so a challenge has a low social cost. A machine-checkable trigger lets a background agent watch the decision, like an SLO alert on a decision.
pending: null
--- body
The agent asks one question at every decision: what must become true to change this decision? The ask is mandatory. A metric in the answer is not.

Answers, from best to weakest:
1. A metric to track. Example: median eSIM install time > 4 min over 7 days, PostHog query X. If the metric does not exist yet, building it becomes part of the decision.
2. A manual test by the author: "I test this myself and see if it works."
3. "No metric, because ..." with a reason.
4. "Revisit at any time." This is a valid answer. It is recorded as such.

A criterion points to a rejected alternative (an :optN node). When it fires, the fallback is already on the map.

Parts, each its own card:
- When and how the agent asks: #kill-ask.
- The shape of a criterion, and the no-metric reasons: #kill-shape.
- What checks a criterion, and when: #kill-trigger.
- What happens when a criterion fires: #kill-fire.

The history of fired and unfired criteria is data about decision quality. It feeds #measure.

Related ideas, not yet cards: supersede instead of overturn, scoped exceptions, soft and hard links, assumptions as separate nodes.
--- children: kill-ask, kill-shape, kill-trigger, kill-fire

=== vi-prop [decided] A change marks the next hop only: direct dependents and direct children
why: A reopen or an amend marks the cards that depend on the changed card directly, and its direct children. A review that leaves a card unchanged stops the mark there. A review that changes the card is a change too, so the mark moves one hop more.
pending: null
--- body
```
  ┌───┐  depends_on  ┌───┐  depends_on  ┌───┐
  │ C │─────────────▶│ B │─────────────▶│ A │◀── reopen or amend
  └───┘              └───┘              └───┘
  marked only if     STALE
  B is amended
```

- A change marks only the links that existed when it happened (#vi-prop-bornstale).
- The mark is derived from the log and never written. A card is stale when a card it depends on, or its parent, changed after the link existed, and the card has no review since.
- A review ends in a confirm or an amend (#rederive-reason).
- A card whose basis is stale waits. It is not stale (#map-wait).

A reopen with reason postponed marks cards paused, not stale. The paused mark reaches every card downstream, at any distance (#pr-wf-paused). A paused card is never reviewed, so a pause that moved one hop would stop at the first card.

=== werk-pane [decided] The chat pane is built and the loop closes
why: Talk in the pane, the map redraws while you read the reply.
pending: null
--- body
Each conversation has one long-lived claude child. The server takes a chat message and streams every message back over the existing SSE channel.

Three things that make it work.

1. The open card is prepended as a compact block built from the map itself when it changes: title, why, kind, status, who, children and depends_on. Every other turn gets a one-line '[still on #id]' reminder (#werk-card-blind). Navigating without typing sends nothing.
2. The default tool allowlist is Read, Edit, Write, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch, and Bash for node, bun, curl, python and `rm -f /tmp/`. The agent maintains the map and edits code (#werk-edits). A server flag narrows it.
3. When the agent runs a werk command, the log changes, a file watcher fires, and every open map reloads. The chat transcript never triggers a redraw.

Verified on 2026-09-02: a message in the pane made the agent write a note on #werk-onechat, the log grew by one line, and the note appeared on the card.

=== vi-sysdiag-grid-gaps [open] What the build does with a grid: refuse, warn, or place
why: The build refuses a grid that breaks a tile rule. It warns, but still renders, when the result is legal and hard to read: a U-turn, or a single edge off a card's middle. It places each label against its own lane. Every rule of this kind is its own decision under this card.
pending: null
--- body
Three kinds of rule, one card each:

- **Refuse.** A grid that breaks a tile rule does not build. The tile rules are on #vi-sysdiag-grid.
- **Warn.** A legal grid that is hard to read still builds, with one warning per case: #vi-sysdiag-grid-uturn, #vi-sysdiag-grid-offcentre.
- **Place.** Where the build puts label text and the line under it: #vi-sysdiag-grid-labelhug, #vi-sysdiag-grid-inline-label.

=== st-build-steps [decided] Build: a builder loop per ticket and a merge loop per run
why: One ticket is built alone in its own worktree. A run merges many tickets into one tree. The two need different loops with different stop conditions.
pending: null
--- body
Build turns a decided subtree into merged, checked code. It runs on two levels.

- **Per ticket:** #st-build-ticket. A builder loop in one worktree: implement, check, grade, and a fresh pass on a fail.
- **Per run:** #st-build-run. A merge loop over the finished tickets: merge one, check the merged tree, run the held-out set.

**Words.** The per-ticket step is "check", not "validate". Validate is the stage that holds what the builder cannot see.
--- children: lp-two, lp-trend, lp-stateless, st-build-ticket, st-build-run, lp-overseer, st-build-seam

werk-wording: proposed

No planning-process narration in a title, why, or body: no "Eryk said", no "the next thing to prove", no comparison to where the conversation stands.

This includes a card's own edit history. "X is new", "Y used to say/name Z", "that no longer holds/applies" still narrate the session, even when the subject is the card itself. State the current fact plainly. The same holds for where the text came from: "moved here from #x", "split out of #y", "merged from #z". The log records the move; the card states the fact.

A reversal is still fair game to record — a superseded card can say what replaced it and why the earlier reading was wrong — but as a fact about the subject, not a play-by-play of the conversation that produced it. Attribution lives in the "who" field and in the log, not in prose.

A card stays at the level of the decision. It names behaviour and concepts. It does not name a command or a flag: the command form of an operation lives on one card under #werk-cli, and every other card names the operation instead. It does not name source files, functions, classes, constants, line numbers, or internal endpoints. Those change with every refactor, and the card would go stale while its decision still holds. The code points to the card, not the other way round.

The map records decisions that hold for any module, not results for one module. Applying a rule to one module — its behaviour list, its coverage threshold, its test plan — produces an artifact, not a decision. That artifact lives next to the code it describes, in the module's own tests. A card for one module is fair only when that module raises a real design fork the general rule cannot settle.

==A card does not list its child cards. The refines edges hold that list, and the map draws it under the card. A copy in the body is a second list that catches up only later: a child that is added, moved, or removed leaves the copy wrong, and no mark shows it. A card states its own higher-level fact. When a sentence states a fact that a child card expands, it names that child in parentheses after the fact. A bullet list or a numbered list in a body is a last resort in general. A list whose items mirror the children is never correct, even when each item is a short fact with the child in parentheses.==
